news_posts.post_content:
If you need to run OLAP queries with low latency,
consider using PostgreSQL 19 on Lakehouse.

Databricks just announced that PostgreSQL 19 is now available on Lakebase.
That means you can spin up a fully managed PostgreSQL instance directly on the lake.
The new version brings native partition pruning,
improved parallelism,
and better JSON handling.
All of these features translate to faster query times on large data sets.

For a data engineer, this opens a simple path to combine transactional consistency with lake‑scale storage.
You can load raw files into the lake,
run transformations with Spark,
and let downstream analytics query the same data through PostgreSQL without moving it.

A practical step is to provision a PostgreSQL 19 cluster from the Databricks UI,
enable the auto‑scaling option,
and point your BI tools to the provided endpoint.
Monitor query latency and adjust the warehouse size as needed.

Give it a try on a non‑critical dataset and see how the built‑in optimizations affect performance.
If the results look good, consider migrating more workloads.

news_posts.post_content:
Imagine you are reviewing a nightly backup and the system suddenly throws a strange error.

On the other hand,
 you believed your database was locked down.

A recent researcher showed remote code execution tricks that work on PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle.

The proof‑of‑concept code runs inside the database engine and can take over the host.

That means a single vulnerable query can turn into a full system compromise.

For us data engineers this is a wake‑up call.

First,
 keep your database versions up to date.

Apply vendor patches as soon as they are released.

Second,
 limit the privileges of the database user that runs application code.

Avoid giving superuser rights unless absolutely necessary.

Third,
 enable network segmentation so that the database is not directly reachable from the internet.

Use firewalls or VPC rules to restrict access to trusted hosts.

Finally,
 monitor logs for unusual commands or spikes in CPU usage.

Even a small change in query pattern can hint at an exploit attempt.

Taking these steps reduces the attack surface and buys you time to respond.

Stay curious,
 stay patched,
 and keep your data pipelines safe.

news_posts.post_content:
When you let an AI control a local computer,
 the biggest risk is unintended access to your files and network.
Google’s Gemini can now issue commands on a Mac,
 acting like a personal assistant that clicks, types, and opens apps,
 as reported by TechCrunch.
Fact: Gemini uses an execution layer that translates natural‑language prompts into OS‑level actions.
Interpretation: This layer is powerful, but it also expands the attack surface if permissions are too broad.
To manage that risk, treat the AI as a privileged service and apply the same controls you would for any script.
Practical checklist:
1. Define the exact tasks the agent may perform.
2. Grant the narrowest OS permissions needed for those tasks.
3. Use sandboxing or user‑level accounts to isolate the agent.
4. Log every command the agent sends and review logs regularly.
5. Set explicit timeouts or revocation mechanisms.
By separating the language model from the execution environment, you keep the model’s flexibility while limiting potential damage.
Recommendation: Before enabling any AI‑driven automation on your workstation, audit the permission set and start with a sandboxed test user.

news_posts.source_article: Google gives Gemini the ability to use your Mac for you - TechCrunch

concept_posts.post_content:
A common implementation mistake is turning on Adaptive Query Execution but leaving the default thresholds unchanged.
Spark then decides to coalesce partitions or switch join types based on data sizes that are no longer accurate.
The result is unnecessary shuffles or even out‑of‑memory errors.

Here’s a quick checklist to make AQE work reliably:

- Enable AQE early in your session: spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true.
- Adjust size‑based thresholds to match your workload, for example spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled=true and set spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.minPartitionSize and spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.maxPartitionSize.
- Turn on skew‑join handling when you know your data has hot keys: spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled=true.

Example scenario: you run a 500 GB aggregation on a cluster with 200 GB of executor memory.
With AQE active, Spark can shrink the number of shuffle partitions after the first stage, saving memory and speeding up the job.

Common mistake to avoid: enabling AQE but forgetting to set spark.sql.adaptive.shuffleTargetPostShuffleInputSize, which can leave you with too many small partitions.

Rule of thumb: after you enable AQE, always review the three adaptive settings above and run a small test job to confirm partition sizes are reasonable.
